title: At The Host in Umhlanga, Durban's Love for Indian Food Meets the Warmth of a Family Home
excerpt: Owner Vivek Moodley sold Durban favourite Mali's, emigrated to Canada and came back — now, with his family and original kitchen team, he is hosting Umhlanga like guests in his own home
body:
• The Host, at 12 Lighthouse Road in Umhlanga Rocks near Durban, is owner Vivek Moodley's return to the restaurant trade after he sold the acclaimed Mali's and emigrated to Canada.
  • Moodley named it The Host because he wants guests to feel invited into his home: 'Once you enter The Host you are family.'
  • The menu spans North and South Indian cooking plus Indo-Chinese dishes, with reviewers singling out the Manchurian mushrooms, lamb pepper fry, prawn Chettinad and potato dosa.
  • Many of the original Mali's team are back in the kitchen, and the chilli crab that made Mali's famous can be ordered in advance.

In Durban, Indian food is not a trend. It is home cooking for one of the largest Indian communities outside India, and it comes with exacting standards. That is the audience The Host set out to win when it opened in Umhlanga, the coastal suburb north of the city — and, by the account of reviewers who have eaten there, it is winning them the way a family home does: with a familiar face at the door.

“We'd heard about a new Indian restaurant in Umhlanga called The Host,” wrote reviewer Frank Chemaly in a review published through IOL's African News Agency. “And we weren't there long before a familiar face came to welcome us to the table. It was Vivek from Mali's, the acclaimed Indian restaurant that for many was Durban's top pick.”

A familiar face returns

Owner Vivek Moodley first opened Mali's in Morningside in 2013, naming it after his father, who owned several local restaurants. He and his family sold Mali's, emigrated to Canada, missed home, and returned to Durban. At The Host, many of the original team are back in the kitchen, working from what Chemaly called their “tried and tested recipe” — with, Moodley insists, improvements.

As SoSuterBill's Billy Suter reported when the restaurant opened at the beginning of July, Moodley chose the name deliberately. “I give personal attention and it's about a host making people feel at home,” he said. “Everyone is not just a number here. Once you enter The Host you are family.” Moodley works the floor alongside his brother Keertan and his cousin Trevor Maistry, and the room — dark wood, white tile, jungle-themed murals and a peacock-inspired bar front — is smart and modern.

North and South on one menu

The Host promises authentic Indian cuisine across both traditions: North Indian curries and tandoor dishes alongside South Indian dosas and Chettinad cooking, plus an Indo-Chinese section. Three seasoned North and South Indian chefs, each with 15 to 20 years of experience, cook dishes fresh to order, Moodley told Suter.

That breadth matters in Durban, where a single table might order across regions without thinking twice. Chemaly's group worked through chicken tikka he called “succulent and moist and beautifully spiced,” spicy papadums loaded with sambals, a mixed vegetable curry with paneer, naan and flaky paratha alongside the mains.

The dishes reviewers keep ordering

Two starters drew the strongest praise in both reviews. The Manchurian mushrooms — crisp battered mushrooms tossed in a sticky, fiery sauce with spring onions — impressed even Moodley, who normally dislikes mushrooms. And the lamb pepper fry was, for Chemaly, “the highlight, rich, still moist yet fired up with pepper and spring onions,” mopped up with paratha and a cooling raita. It also carried a memory: a late friend from Johannesburg who, after sharing the dish in Mali's early days, brought the whole Joburg bridge group back to pack the restaurant out on every Durban trip.

Among the curries, each had its own distinct flavour, Chemaly found: a balanced lamb rogan josh, prawns in the fiery pepper-and-chilli flavours of Chettinad, and a potato dosa — the large, crisp rice pancake stuffed with potato curry — arriving at almost every table. Mali's was famed for its chilli crab; The Host does not keep it on the daily menu, but crab curry fans can order it in advance so it can be made fresh. Dessert, in both reviews, ended the same way: homemade kulfi, creamy and not overly sweet.

If you go

The Host is at 12 Lighthouse Road, Umhlanga Rocks, across from the Radisson Hotel. The review listing gives hours as daily 12.30pm to 10pm, closed Tuesdays, and bookings and advance crab orders on 076 780 8339. Chemaly's scores were Food 4, Service 3 and Ambience 3½, with a bill of R2412 for five. For Durban's Indian diaspora — and for anyone visiting Umhlanga who wants to understand why this city's Indian table sets such a high bar — The Host is less a comeback than a homecoming, served one family-style welcome at a time.

nri_angle: Durban is home to one of the largest Indian diaspora communities in the world, and its restaurants are judged against home cooking. The Host tells a classic diaspora story in reverse: a Durban-born Indian restaurateur who emigrated to Canada, missed home, and returned to reopen with his family and original team.
